clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder in which affected males have intellectual disability with a distinctive combination of obesity and hypogonadism
Facial features include a coarse face with a prominent supraorbital ridge, deep-set eyes, large ears and narrow palpebral fissures
Truncal obesity, gynaecomastia, small genitalia and delayed or absent puberty reflect the hypogonadism
The fingers are typically tapered and the toes short, and there may be shortened metacarpals or metatarsals
Carrier females may show milder, variable features influenced by X-inactivation
Caused by variants in PHF6, encoding a chromatin-associated protein of the PHD-finger family involved in transcriptional regulation
The phenotype overlaps other obesity-hypogonadism syndromes, so it is easily misclassified
reference.pathophysiology: PHF6 encodes a plant homeodomain (PHD) finger protein that localises to the nucleus and nucleolus and participates in chromatin-associated transcriptional regulation, including interactions with chromatin-remodelling and ribosome-biogenesis machinery. Loss-of-function variants impair this transcriptional control during development of the brain and endocrine tissues, producing intellectual disability together with the hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction that underlies the obesity and hypogonadism. As an X-linked gene, PHF6 variants affect males more consistently, while carrier females show variable expression. The combined effect on neuronal and endocrine gene expression accounts for the characteristic syndromic picture.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital leptin or melanocortin pathway obesity disorders
additionalInvestigations: Endocrine evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and pubertal status
Assessment of obesity and its metabolic complications
Skeletal imaging of hands and feet for shortened digits and tapering
Targeted PHF6 sequencing or an X-linked intellectual-disability gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Complications of severe obesity such as obstructive sleep apnoea
Absent or arrested puberty requiring endocrine management
reference.prognosis: Affected males have lifelong intellectual disability with obesity and hypogonadism that require ongoing endocrine and metabolic management; carrier females are usually more mildly affected. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as Prader-Willi or another obesity syndrome without genetic confirmation
Overlooking milder features in carrier females
Neglecting endocrine evaluation of delayed puberty
Attributing obesity to lifestyle alone and missing the syndromic diagnosis
management: No disease-specific therapy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary
Endocrine management of the hypogonadism, including testosterone or hormone replacement and induction of puberty in affected males
Weight management and treatment of obesity-related metabolic complications
Developmental and educational support for the intellectual disability
Ongoing endocrine, metabolic and skeletal monitoring
X-linked genetic counselling with carrier assessment of female relatives
